translations.text: In the second year of the reign

of Artaxerxes the great king, on the first day of the month of Adar, which is Areg in Armenian, Mordecai, son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Jewish man, saw a vision.
He lived in the city of Susa, a prominent man who was trustworthy in all the affairs of the king’s household.
He was one of the captives whom Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians, had taken captive from Jerusalem along with Jeconiah, king of Judea.
This is the dream vision he saw: a sound of turmoil, thunder, and earthquakes, and there was great turmoil upon the earth.
And behold, two exceedingly great dragons came forward, ready to fight one another.
A great sound came from them, and at the sound of their cry all the nations prepared for war, to wage war against the righteous nation.
It was a day of darkness and gloom, suffering and distress, and there was great turmoil upon the earth.
The whole righteous nation was troubled because of their calamities, and they prepared for destruction and cried out to God.
And from the sound of their voices there came a great, clear river, as though from a small spring.
The sun rose, and the lowly were exalted and devoured the mighty.

Mordecai awoke from this vision of what God intended to do. He kept the dream vision in his heart and wanted with all his strength to understand what the vision he had seen that very night might mean.
Mordecai stayed in the palace with Dabith and Terah, the king’s two eunuchs who guarded the king’s palace.
When Mordecai learned of the eunuchs’ plans and examined the intentions of their hearts, discovering that they were preparing to lay hands on King Artaxerxes, he revealed their plans to the king.
The king questioned the two eunuchs, and they confessed to him, and he ordered them to be bound.
The king wrote these matters in the records, and Mordecai also wrote about these matters.
The king ordered Mordecai to take even greater care in looking after the king’s household, and he gave him gifts.
Haman, son of Hammedatha the Bougaean, was held in honor before the king, and he wished to torment Mordecai and his people because of the two eunuchs.
After these events, in the days of Artaxerxes—this Artaxerxes ruled over one hundred and twenty-seven provinces, from India to Ethiopia—
in those days when he sat enthroned in the city of Susa,
In the third year of his reign, the king gave a banquet for his friends and nobles, and also for others from the peoples of Persia and Media and for all the rulers and provincial governors.
he displayed to them the greatness of his kingdom and the glorious delight of his splendor for one hundred and eighty days.
When the days of the banquet came to an end, he again ordered that the common people of his city be invited to a banquet in the courtyard of the royal house for six days.

It was decorated with fine linen and cotton cloth, which had been arranged and secured with cords of purple and fine linen and fastened to gold and purple capitals that stood on precious columns and golden bases. There were many gold and silver seats, inlaid with pearls and precious stones and furnished with coverings, multicolored designs, and costly fabrics, in the rose-paved courtyard.
There were the king’s golden and silver jars and drinking vessels, worth thirty thousand talents, and an abundance of wine fit for the king to drink.
The banquet took place according to custom, for this was how the king wished to treat the servants attending him.
Vashti, the king’s wife, held a banquet for the women in the palace of King Artaxerxes.
On the seventh day, the king was merry at heart and spoke to Aman, Bazan, Terah, Buraze, Atheltha, Batenza, and Tharabba, the seven eunuchs who attended him.
to summon the woman to the royal court, make her queen, and show all the princes and peoples her beauty, for she was very beautiful.
But Vashti would not obey him and come to him with the eunuchs. The king was distressed and became very angry.
He told his friends what Vashti had done. “Now,” said the king, “establish laws and judgments from this point onward.”
Arkesaeus, Arnather, and Maliseear, princes of the Persians and Medes who were close to the king and shared his throne, came before him.
They asked what the law required them to do to Vashti, the king’s wife, because she had not carried out the king’s commands, which he had sent to her through the eunuchs.
Memucan said to the king and the princes, “Vashti, the queen of queens, has defied not only the king but also all the king’s princes and governors.
In the same way, all women will become disobedient to the princes of the Persians and Medes.
When they hear of the contempt shown by this king’s wife, they will dare to dominate and dishonor their husbands.
Now, if the king wishes and finds it pleasing, let her no longer come before the king, and let him give her position as queen to a woman better than she is.
They will hear the laws you decree throughout your kingdom, and women will show their husbands great honor, from the poor to the nobles.”
The proposal pleased the king and all his princes, and the king did as Memucan had said.
He sent throughout his kingdom, to every province, in accordance with the decree imposed on all women.
After these events, the king’s anger subsided, and he no longer remembered Vashti, for he kept in mind what she had said. Thus the woman was rejected and cast out.
And the king’s servants said, “Let beautiful young virgins be sought for the king.”

“Let the king order governors to be appointed throughout the whole land of your kingdom. Let them select young virgin girls and have them brought to the city of Susa, to one house for virgins. Let them entrust them to the royal eunuch who is the keeper of the women, and let the king order that they be given oil, ointments, and every treatment.
Let the woman who pleases the king become queen in Vashti’s place.” These proposals pleased the king, and he did so.
There was a Jewish man in the city of Susa named Mordecai, son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin.
He had been brought captive from Jerusalem, which Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians, had taken captive.

He had brought up a child, the daughter of Amminadab, his father’s brother. Her name was Esther. When he took her from her mother and father, he intended to take her as his wife. The girl was very beautiful to look at.
When the king’s command became known, many girls were gathered in the city of Susa under Hegai’s care. They brought Esther to Hegai, the eunuch in charge of the women.

The girl pleased him and found favor with him. He hurried to give her ointments and her allotted treatments, along with the seven girls who had been given to her from the royal court as maids. He cared for Esther more than for her other companions, and likewise for her maids.
Esther did not reveal her people or her province, because Mordecai had instructed her not to tell.
Every day Mordecai would walk around near the house of the women to see what was happening to Esther.

For the time was approaching for the girl to go in to the king, when twelve months had been completed. This was how they completed their days of treatment: for six months they were anointed with fragrant oils, and for six months they received fragrant incense, ointments, and the washing prescribed for women.
Then she would go in to the king, and whoever she wished to be entrusted to would go with her into the chamber before the king.

In the evening she would go in to the king, and during the day she would return to her companions and to Hegai, the eunuch in charge of the women. She remained there until she was called [?] into the king’s chamber.

When the time came for Esther, the daughter of Aminadab, the brother of Mordecai’s father, to go in to the king, she disregarded none of the instructions given to her by the eunuch in charge of the women. Esther had found favor with everyone who saw her.
Esther went in to the king in the twelfth month, Adar, which in Armenian is Areg, in the seventh year of his reign.
Esther pleased the king greatly, and she found favor with him above all the other women. He placed the women’s crown on her head.
The king held a feast for all his friends and his troops for seven days. He honored Esther’s wedding and ordered that a remission be granted to everyone under his rule.
Mordecai looked after the king’s household and kept it in order.

But Esther did not disclose the country of her native province, for Mordecai had instructed her to fear God and obey his commands, just as she had done when she was with him before. Esther did not change her way of life.

And two of the king’s eunuchs, who were chief guards of the people, became distressed because they were jealous of Mordecai, whom the king honored more than them, and they wanted to kill King Artaxerxes.
Mordecai was informed of this matter and made it known to Esther, and Esther disclosed the murderous plot to the king.
The king rebuked the two eunuchs and hanged them on a wooden gallows. The king ordered that the matter be carefully recorded, including how Mordecai had been faithful to him.
After this, King Artaxerxes honored Haman, together with Dathuba and his companions, and raised him to the foremost seat above all his friends.
Everyone in the king’s household bowed down to him, because the king had ordered them to do so. But Mordecai did not bow down to him.
The king’s officials spoke to Mordecai and said, “Mordecai, why do you not bow down to Haman as the king commanded?”
They spoke to him every day, but he would not listen to them, so they accused Mordecai before Haman. Mordecai did not obey the king’s commands because he was a Jew.
When Haman learned that Mordecai would not bow down to him, he became very angry.
He devised a plan to destroy the Jews who were under the rule of King Artaxerxes.

They conducted a reckoning in the twelfth year of Artaxerxes’ reign, and he cast lots day by day and month by month to determine how to destroy Mordecai’s people in a single day. The lot fell on the fourteenth of the month of Adar.

And he spoke to the king and said, “There is a people scattered among the nations throughout your kingdom. They are more wicked and deceitful than all other peoples, and they do not obey the royal laws. It is of no benefit to the king if you let them remain.”
“Now, if it pleases the king, give an order to destroy them, and I will deposit ten thousand talents of silver in the royal treasury.”
The king took off his ring and placed it in Haman’s hands, to write concerning the Jews and seal the document for their destruction.
The king said to Haman, “Keep your silver, and do whatever you wish with that people.”

And the royal scribes were summoned in the first month, on the thirteenth day. As Haman commanded them, they wrote a letter to the military commanders and governors throughout all the provinces, from India to Ethiopia, one hundred and twenty-seven provinces, and to the rulers of the peoples, each in its own language, by order of Artaxerxes.

The letters were sent by messengers throughout Artaxerxes’ entire realm, ordering the destruction of the Jewish people in a single day in the twelfth month, which is Adar, and the plundering of all their goods and possessions.
The decree in the letter was as follows:

When Mordecai learned what had happened, he tore his robe, put on sackcloth, and scattered ashes over his head. He went through the city’s public squares, crying out loudly and saying, “Why, then, are you destroying my people without cause, [?], unjustly, when they have done nothing evil?”
He came as far as the gates of the royal house and stopped there, because he was not permitted to enter the royal courtyard wearing sackcloth and ashes.
Throughout all the provinces, wherever the letter was read, there was an outcry, lamentation, and great mourning among the Jews, and they covered themselves with sackcloth and ashes.

The eunuchs and the maidservants of the queen, the lady of ladies, came in and told Esther. She was deeply troubled when she heard about the command the king had given. She sent clothes for Mordecai to put on and ordered his sackcloth to be taken off, but he would not agree.
Esther called Hathach, her eunuch, who was always in attendance before her, and sent him to find out from Mordecai whether it was really so.
Mordecai explained to him what had happened and the promise Haman had made to give the king ten thousand talents for the treasury so that he would destroy the Jews.

He also gave the eunuch a copy of the decree that had been read in the city of Susa for their destruction, so that he could show it to Esther. He instructed him to tell her, “Go in and petition the king and plead for the people. Remember the days of your hardship, when you were brought up in my care. For Haman, who is second to the king, has spoken against us to bring about our death. Now pray earnestly to the Lord God, speak to your king on our behalf, and save us from this death.”
Hathach went in and told her these words.
Esther said to Hathach, “Go to Mordecai and tell him:

‘All the people of this kingdom know that any man or woman who enters the king’s inner chamber without being summoned has no escape, unless the king extends the golden scepter to that person. Only that person lives. But I have not been summoned to enter the king’s presence for thirty days now.’”
Hathach reported all Esther’s words to Mordecai.
Mordecai said to Hathach, “Go and tell her, ‘Esther, do not say to yourself that you alone of all the Jews will survive in this kingdom.

If you do not listen at this time, help and deliverance will come to the Jews from elsewhere, but you and your father’s household will perish. And who knows whether you became queen for this very time?’”
Esther sent another message to Mordecai and said:

“Go and gather the Jews who are in the city of Susa, and fast for me. Do not eat or drink for three days, either by day or by night. My maids and I will also take care to fast, and then I will go in to the king. Although doing this is contrary to the king’s laws, I will do it; and even if I must die, I will not delay.”
Mordecai went and did as Esther had instructed him.
I, the great king Artaxerxes, write this to you governors and rulers in the regions of India and Ethiopia, to those subject to you, and to the whole land.

I wished to govern not with anger and arrogance over my power, but with kindness and humility, to keep the lives of those under my authority secure at all times and, with the kingdom at peace to the ends of the earth, to renew the peace that all people have desired.

I trusted my counselors concerning how this matter should be brought to completion. Haman had shown wisdom and care with unwavering, steadfast loyalty, and through this had become worthy of sharing my throne as second in rank.

He informed us that throughout the whole world a hostile people is mixed among the nations, obstructing the laws. They oppose kings and reject their commands, refusing to obey those that we have established and confirmed for the security of our rule.

Now, taking this people alone, with their entire nation, before all people, whoever they may be, [?] to abolish the practices of foreign laws. They are hostile and opposed to our affairs; every evil is carried out by their hands, and they are enemies of our kingdom.

We have now decreed, and therefore have informed you by this letter of ours and through Haman, who has been appointed over these affairs and is our second father, that all of them, together with their wives and children, are to be destroyed and cut down by the sword of their enemies, without pity or mercy, on the fourth day of the twelfth month, which is Adar.
In this year they shall descend to Hades in a single day by a cruel death, and after that time we shall have peace, once these things have been accomplished.

Copies of the decrees were written and distributed throughout all the provinces, and when that command went out, everyone made preparations for that day. These measures quickly reached the city of Susa as well. The king and Haman indulged themselves in luxury, while the whole city was in turmoil.
He pleaded with the Lord in prayer, calling to mind and remembering the Lord’s mighty deeds, and said:
“Lord God, almighty King, everyone awaits your command. No one can stand against you when you wish to save your people Israel.
For you, Lord, made heaven and earth and all wondrous things.
You rule over everything, and no one can oppose your dominion, you who know everything.
For it was not out of pride, arrogance, or contempt that I did this, refusing to bow down to the arrogant Haman.
Rather, I would gladly have kissed the heels of his feet to save the house of Israel.
But I will do this so that I may not give glory to a human being, but to you alone, the true God. I will bow down to no one except you, my Lord, and I did not do this out of arrogance.
Now, Lord, God of Abraham, spare your people, for destroyers have risen against us and desire to destroy your inheritance, which has been yours from the beginning.
Do not disregard your portion, which you redeemed for yourself from the land of the Egyptians.

Hear, Lord, the sound of my prayers, and be merciful to your inheritance. Turn our mourning into joy, so that we who are alive may bless your name, great Lord. Do not destroy the mouths of those who bless you.”
All Israel cried out to the Lord with all their strength, for death was before them.
Queen Esther took refuge in the Lord and was gripped by great anguish.

She took off her glorious royal garments and put on sackcloth of affliction and mourning. Instead of the various precious oils and perfumes, she covered her head with ashes and dung. She humbled her body with many hardships and covered every place she had adorned for her delight with the locks of her hair.
She came before the Lord, the God of Israel, with many prayers and petitions, pleading with him and saying, “My Lord and our King, you alone help me, who am alone and have no helper except you,
for great danger lies before me.

From my birth I have heard from my ancestral people that you, Lord, chose Israel from all the nations, and our fathers from their lineage, as your inheritance forever, and did for them everything you promised. And again, continuing at length in her prayers, she said: “God of Abraham, God of Isaac, and God of Jacob, you are blessed forever. I have heard from the writings of my ancestors that you, Lord, transferred Enoch from earth to heaven, from repentance to eternal life. I have heard from the writings of my ancestors, Lord, that you saved Noah from the waters of the flood. I have heard from the writings of my ancestors, Lord, that you gave Abraham glory before his men, among kings. I have heard from the writings of my ancestors, Lord, that you saved Jonah from the great fish. I have heard from the writings of my ancestors, Lord, that you rescued the three young men from the fiery furnace and saved Daniel from the lions’ den. I have heard from the writings of my ancestors, Lord, that you rescued Hezekiah, king of Judea, when he was condemned to death, and when he prayed to you for his life, you had mercy, granted his request, and added fifteen years to his life. I have heard from the writings of my ancestors, Lord, that when Hannah sought you, Lord, with prayers and petitions, you granted her a child, the great Samuel.
And now, Lord, we have sinned before you, and you have delivered us into the hands of our enemies.
In return for our glorifying their gods, you are just, Lord.
And they were not satisfied with our serving them, but laid their hands upon their idols,
to abolish what your mouth decreed, destroy your inheritance, silence the mouths that bless you, and extinguish the glory of your house and your holy altar,
and open the mouths of the nations to glorify their worthless gods and glorify the mortal kings of this age.

And now, Lord God, do not deliver your allotted inheritance into the hands of those who are nothing at all, lest they rejoice and exult over our destruction. Instead, turn their schemes back upon them, and disgrace the one who has risen against us.
Remember, Lord, and do not overlook us in this time of our distress. Give me courage, you who are King of all kings and Lord of lords,
and put pleasing words in my mouth, through which I may find favor before the king. Turn his heart to hatred of our enemy, so that he and those who side with him may be slaughtered.
But save us with your uplifted arm, and help me, who am alone and have no helper except you, Lord.
Lord, you know and recognize everyone’s heart. I have hated the glory of these lawless people, and I loathe the bed of these uncircumcised people and all these foreign possessions.
You know my predicament, Lord: the crown upon my head is repulsive to me. I loathe it like a cloth used during a woman’s monthly period, and I do not wear it when I remain indoors.
And your maidservant has not eaten from Haman’s table, nor have I honored the king’s drinking feasts, nor have I drunk the wine of their sacrifices.
And your servant has found no joy from the day I entered the king’s presence until now, except in you, Lord, Lord God of Abraham.
God, mighty over all, hear the voices of us who have no hope. Rescue us from the hands of those who torment us, deliver me from the terror that I fear, and save your people Israel.
